html:
The map's name, in its 1880 snapshot, for the mobile state of the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr (about 1840 to 1900), who conquered his way from the upper Nile basin to Lake Chad. In 1880 he was still in the borderlands of what are now South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

Rabih served under the slave trader al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur in the Bahr el Ghazal. When Egyptian forces crushed Zubayr's son in 1879, Rabih led part of the army west. Raiding for slaves and ivory, he grew from a few hundred men to an army of thousands and defeated Bagirmi.

In 1893 he conquered Bornu, ended its old dynasty, and ruled it harshly from his new capital at Dikwa. He then blocked French plans to link their African colonies. At the battle of Kousseri in April 1900 a French force defeated and killed him; the French commander, Lamy, also died, and the town of Fort-Lamy, today's N'Djamena, was named after him.
